type-perennial: Border perennials are the workhorses of a planted scheme: they die back each winter and return reliably from the crown, so the framework you set holds for years. Improve the whole bed with garden compost before planting rather than spot-feeding individual holes, and plant in groups of three or five of one variety so they read as a drift rather than dotted singletons. Space at roughly two-thirds of the eventual spread; they knit together by the second summer. The commonest mistake is planting everything at one height, which gives a flat, lumpy bed. Lift and divide clumps every three or four years to keep them vigorous. The perennials listed here cover that backbone, from front-of-border fillers to substantial clump-formers.
type-shrub: Shrubs give a border its bones. Because they are woody and permanent they decide the scale and winter shape of the whole scheme, so place them first and let the perennials flow around them. Dig a square planting hole, tease out any pot-bound roots, and plant at the same depth the shrub sat in its container; firm well and water in. Allow for the mature spread on the label, not the nursery size, or you will be cutting things back hard within a few years. Mulch the root zone but keep mulch off the stems. Group flowering shrubs with evergreens so there is structure once the flowers have gone. These shrubs range from compact front-of-border types to larger backbone plants.
type-bulb: Bulbs are the cheapest way to extend a border's season, flowering when little else is awake and then retreating underground. Plant most at roughly two to three times their own depth, pointed end up, in groups rather than rows; informal clusters of ten or more look natural where soldierly lines do not. Sharp drainage matters most, so add grit on heavy ground or they sit wet and rot. Resist tidying the foliage until it has yellowed, as the leaves are feeding next year's flower. Interplant with later perennials that will hide the dying leaves. These bulbs span spring, summer and autumn flowering, so you can layer them for succession.
type-grass: Ornamental grasses bring movement, see-through texture and a long season that carries a border well into winter. Most prefer an open position and free-draining soil; on rich, wet ground they flop. Divide the timing of your cut-back by type: deciduous grasses are sheared to the base in late winter, while evergreens are simply combed through with gloved hands to pull out the dead. Plant in generous swathes and let them mingle with upright perennials so the seed heads catch low light. The frequent error is dotting single specimens, which looks accidental. These grasses cover both the airy, transparent kinds and the denser, mound-forming types.
type-annual: Annuals complete their whole life in one season, which makes them the fastest way to fill gaps, trial colour combinations, or carry a young border while the permanent planting establishes. Sow or plant after the last frost, deadhead regularly, and they will flower for months on end; left to set seed, most stop. They are hungry and thirsty, so a feed every fortnight and consistent watering pays off. Use them in drifts between perennials rather than as standalone bedding blocks, which can look municipal. Many are excellent for pollinators and for cutting. The annuals listed here are chosen to weave through a mixed border rather than sit in regimented rows.
type-climber: Climbers earn their keep by gardening upwards, clothing fences, walls, obelisks and arches that would otherwise be dead space. Match the plant to its support: twiners need wires or trellis to wind around, while self-clinging types attach directly to masonry. Plant a good 30cm out from the base of a wall, where the soil is dry in the rain shadow, and lean the stems back towards their support. Prune to the habit, as flowering time dictates when you cut. The usual mistake is letting a vigorous climber loose on a flimsy frame. These climbers run from restrained, well-mannered choices to robust coverers for a larger structure.
full-sun: A sunny, south or west-facing aspect with six or more hours of direct light suits the widest range of flowering plants, but it also dries fastest and bakes hardest in high summer. Many sun-lovers actually prefer lean, sharp-draining soil; overfeeding gives soft, floppy growth that needs staking. Mulch to hold moisture, water deeply but infrequently to send roots down, and avoid crowding so air moves freely and foliage stays dry. The classic error is choosing plants that scorch, so favour those with grey, hairy or waxy leaves built to cope with glare. The plants here are selected to thrive in open sun and to keep flowering through the heat.
shade: A north-facing border or the shadow of a building need not be a problem; it simply asks for a different palette built on foliage as much as flower. Dry shade under trees is the hardest case, so enrich the soil heavily with leaf mould and compost and water new plants through their first two summers until they root down. Lean on contrasting leaf shapes and the many shades of green for interest, with white and pale flowers to lift the gloom. The common mistake is forcing sun-lovers into shade, where they stretch and sulk. The plants listed here are genuinely happy out of direct sun, including reliable performers for dry ground beneath established trees.
partial-shade: An east-facing border or dappled light beneath open-canopy trees offers the gentlest growing conditions: morning sun, then shelter from the fierce midday glare. Many woodland-edge plants are at their best here, flowering well without scorching. The one hazard is the early sun striking frosted buds on a cold spring morning, so avoid the most frost-tender flowers in an east-facing spot. Keep the soil moisture-retentive with compost, since dappled sites can still dry under a tree canopy. Combine bold foliage with airy flowers to make the most of the moving light. These plants suit that in-between aspect, content with a few hours of sun and shade the rest of the day.
soil-clay: Heavy clay is cold and slow to warm in spring, sticky when wet and rock-hard when dry, but it is fertile and holds nutrients well once you work with it. Never dig or plant when it is waterlogged, as you will smear the structure into an airless pan. Open it up with coarse grit and bulky organic matter forked into the top spit, and plant in autumn or spring when it is moist but workable. Plant slightly proud and mulch thickly. Many robust, deep-rooting plants relish clay's reserves of moisture and food. The choices here are tough customers that establish well in heavy ground and will not rot off in a wet winter.
soil-sandy: Free-draining sand warms early and is easy to dig, but water and nutrients drain straight through, so plants dry out and starve unless you intervene. Bulk it up every year with garden compost and well-rotted manure to build moisture-holding humus, and mulch generously to slow evaporation. Plant in spring so roots establish before the next dry spell, and water new plants regularly until they settle. The mistake is treating sand like loam and expecting it to hold a feed. Many Mediterranean and coastal plants positively prefer this sharp drainage and resent richer ground. The plants here are chosen to cope with quick-draining soil and the drought it brings.
soil-chalk: Thin soil over chalk is alkaline, often shallow and stony, and drains very freely, so it dries out fast and locks up iron, which can yellow unsuitable plants. Forget acid-lovers such as rhododendrons; instead choose lime-tolerant plants that revel in the open, alkaline conditions. Add organic matter every year to deepen the topsoil and hold moisture over the chalk, and mulch to protect shallow roots. Plant firmly and water in well, as stony ground can leave air pockets. Many fragrant, nectar-rich plants are native to chalk downland and thrive here. The plants listed are reliably happy on alkaline ground and will not languish reaching for iron they cannot get.
soil-acid: Acid soil, with a pH below about 6.5, opens the door to a whole group of ericaceous plants that simply will not grow on lime: rhododendrons, azaleas, camellias, pieris, Japanese acers and the heathers. Keep it that way by mulching with leaf mould, composted bark or ericaceous matter, and avoid mushroom compost or lime. Many of these plants are woodland natives that also want shelter and a moisture-retentive, humus-rich root run, so combine acid-loving with shade-tolerant where the two overlap. Do not let the ground dry out in summer. The plants here are selected to make the most of acid ground, from spring-flowering shrubs to autumn-colour specimens.
soil-wet: Permanently moist or boggy ground, where water sits after rain, drowns most border plants by starving their roots of air, but a distinct group of moisture-lovers thrives in exactly these conditions. Distinguish true bog from simple winter wet: very few plants tolerate standing water year round, while many enjoy a soil that never fully dries. Improve drainage only if you mean to change the planting; otherwise embrace it. Bold, lush foliage is the signature of a damp border, so play big leaves against vertical flower spikes. The mistake is planting drought-lovers that promptly rot. These plants are chosen for ground that stays reliably moist, including the margins of a pond or ditch.
evergreen: Evergreens are the quiet framework that holds a garden together through winter, when deciduous planting has retreated to bare earth. Use them to anchor the corners of a border, screen a boundary, or repeat down a bed as a unifying thread. Plant in autumn or spring and water through the first year, as evergreens lose moisture through their leaves even in cold weather and can scorch in a dry, windy winter. Resist the urge to plant only dark green; vary leaf size, texture and the gold or silver-variegated forms. The mistake is a solid wall of one conifer. These plants provide year-round structure, from clippable backbone shrubs to lower furnishing foliage.
pollinator-friendly: A border that feeds bees and butterflies needs nectar and pollen across the longest possible season, not just a midsummer flush, so aim for something in flower from early spring through to the last warm days of autumn. Favour open, single flowers over blowsy doubles, which often hide or lack their pollen, and plant in generous drifts so foraging insects do not waste energy hunting single blooms. Avoid pesticides, and leave some seed heads standing over winter. A sunny, sheltered position keeps insects active and feeding. Native and near-native plants tend to support the widest range of species. The plants here are chosen as genuine nectar sources, sequenced to keep the table laid through the seasons.
pet-safe: If cats and dogs share your garden, it is worth knowing which border plants are non-toxic, since several popular favourites, including foxgloves, lily, yew and daffodil bulbs, are genuinely poisonous if chewed. Young, bored or curious animals are most at risk, particularly with bulbs that look like a digging prize. The plants gathered here are not known to be toxic to cats and dogs, though no plant should be a substitute for fresh grass, and any animal that eats large quantities of greenery may still be sick. Plant densely so there is less bare soil to dig, and site the more delicate choices out of the main run of traffic. These selections let you plant a full border with cats and dogs in mind.
colour-white: A white border reads as cool, calm and luminous, and it comes into its own at dusk, when white flowers glow long after stronger colours have gone flat. White is never quite one colour, so play cream against pure white against the green-whites, and lean heavily on silver and variegated foliage to stop the scheme looking like spilt milk. Green is the essential partner that gives white its freshness. The risk is a tired, browning look, so deadhead diligently, as spent white flowers show every blemish. Site a white scheme where you sit in the evening to get the most from it. These plants are chosen for clean white and palest cream flowers across the seasons.
colour-pink: Pink is the most forgiving border colour, ranging from sharp cerise and magenta through to the softest blush, and it sits happily alongside almost anything. The key decision is warm versus cool: blue-pinks read cool and pair with purple and silver, while salmon and coral pinks read warm and sit better with apricot and bronze. Mixing the two carelessly is what makes a pink scheme jar. Soften strong pinks with plenty of green and grey foliage, and use the palest shades to link bolder colours. Deadhead to keep the flush going. These plants cover the full pink range, so you can build a tonal scheme or pick out a single shade to repeat.
colour-purple: Purple gives a border depth and richness, reading as both restful and slightly dramatic depending on the partners you choose. The classic pairing is purple with yellow or lime, which are opposite on the colour wheel and so make each other sing; for a quieter effect, blend purple into blue and pink for a smoky, hazy band. Dark purple flowers can vanish against soil or shadow, so set them where light catches them or back them with silver foliage. Purple-leaved plants extend the theme long after the flowers fade. These plants run from pale lavender through to the deepest violet, giving you the range to build a considered purple scheme.
colour-yellow: Yellow is the brightest, most advancing colour in the border, full of warmth and energy, and it carries light into shady corners better than any other. That brilliance is also its difficulty: hard, acid yellows can dominate and clash with pinks, so decide early between cool lemon-yellows and warm golden-yellows and keep largely to one camp. Lime-green foliage and blue or purple flowers are yellow's best companions. Use it to lead the eye or to lift a dull spot, but spread it through the bed rather than clumping it all in one glaring block. These plants span soft primrose to rich gold, across spring, summer and autumn, so you can place yellow with intention.
colour-blue: True blue is the rarest and most coveted flower colour, and a blue border feels cool, receding and serene, seeming to push the boundary further away. Most so-called blues lean towards purple or mauve, so check flowers in the ground rather than trusting a catalogue photograph. Blue glows beside its complementary orange and warms up next to yellow; against grey foliage it turns misty and soft. Because blue recedes, mass it generously or it disappears at a distance. The mistake is expecting a sky-blue that few hardy plants truly deliver. These plants are the closest to genuine blue available to UK gardeners, from spring bulbs to late-summer spires.
colour-red: Red is the boldest, hottest colour in the border, demanding attention and bringing drama, but it needs handling with confidence or not at all. Scarlet and orange-reds belong in a hot scheme with bronze foliage, while the cooler crimson and blood-reds sit better with purple and deep pink. Red advances strongly, so a little goes a long way; dotted thinly it looks like a mistake, while massed it reads as deliberate. Dark red flowers, like the richest dahlias, can be lost without a lighter backdrop, so place them against silver or lime. These plants gather the full range of reds, from clear scarlet to velvety near-black crimson, for a scheme with real heat.
colour-green: Green flowers and foliage are the most sophisticated note in a border, prized for their calm, their freshness and the way they set off every other colour around them. A predominantly green scheme relies on contrast of form and texture rather than colour: broad against narrow leaves, glossy against matt, fine fern against bold paddle. Green flowers, found in hellebores, euphorbias and certain tobacco plants, read as quietly unusual and stop a planting looking too sweet. Variegation and lime-green foliage extend the theme. The skill is in the staging rather than the shade. These plants are chosen for genuinely green flowers and for the structural foliage that gives a green-led border its quiet authority.
colour-orange: Orange is pure warmth, the colour of late summer and autumn, and it brings exuberance to a border that cooler schemes can lack. It is also one of the trickiest to place, clashing badly with pink but glowing against its complementary blue and harmonising beautifully with yellow, bronze and chocolate foliage. Commit to it fully in a hot scheme rather than letting a single orange flower fight the rest of the bed. Apricot and soft tangerine shades are gentler and easier to blend than hard pumpkin-orange. These plants range from soft apricot through to fiery scarlet-orange, giving you the palette for a warm, late-season border that builds towards autumn.
style-cottage: The cottage garden is a romantic, generous muddle: roses tumbling over self-seeding hardy annuals, foxgloves rising through hollyhocks, with barely a glimpse of bare soil. The art is in the apparent lack of art, so plant densely, mix flowers with herbs and even vegetables, and let things lean and seed about. Avoid straight rows and rigid blocks, which break the spell. A cottage scheme leans heavily on old-fashioned perennials, fragrant roses and informal climbers, with succession planting so something is always coming into flower. Soft pinks, blues, whites and the odd hot accent suit the mood. These plants are the traditional cottage-garden staples that give a border that abundant, comfortably overgrown character.
style-wildlife: A wildlife border works on every level of the garden at once: nectar and pollen for insects, seed and berries for birds, cover for shelter, and undisturbed corners for hibernation. The aim is abundance and continuity rather than tidiness, so plant a long succession of single, open flowers, include berrying shrubs, and resist the autumn urge to cut everything down, as seed heads and hollow stems feed and house wildlife through winter. A patch left a little wild does more good than a manicured one. Layer the planting from groundcover up to small trees to create habitat at different heights. These plants are chosen to provide food and shelter across the year for the widest range of garden creatures.
style-native: A native border is planted with British wild species, which underpin the food web far more completely than exotics because native insects evolved alongside them. Think hawthorn and hazel for structure, foxglove, primrose and field scabious for flower, bluebell and wood anemone for spring. Match the plant to the wild habitat it comes from: woodland-edge species want some shade and leaf-rich soil, while meadow natives want open sun and lean ground. Resist the temptation to fill a gap with a near-native cultivar, which dilutes the purpose. Allow self-seeding and a looser, more naturalistic hand than a conventional border. These plants are genuine British natives, selected to support local wildlife while still earning their place in a garden.
style-woodland: A woodland border recreates the layered shade beneath trees, where the action happens at ground level in spring before the canopy closes over. The foundation is leaf mould: woodland soil is rich, moisture-retentive and humus-laden, so mulch heavily with composted leaves and never let it bake dry. Plant spring ephemerals that flower and feed early, then carpeting groundcover and bold foliage to hold interest through the shaded summer. Layer from canopy down through shrub to ground. The mistake is leaving bare soil, which dries and weeds; a woodland floor should be densely furnished. These plants are chosen for dappled and full shade with that cool, leafy root run, from early flowers to season-long foliage.
style-modern: A modern border is built on restraint, structure and repetition rather than the floral abundance of a cottage scheme. A limited plant palette, repeated in bold drifts, gives the calm, intentional look; grasses and architectural foliage carry the design, with flower used as a controlled accent rather than the main event. Strong, simple shapes and a quiet colour range, often greens, whites and a single accent, do the work. The mistake is too many different plants, which reads as busy and undermines the clean effect. Pay attention to form, line and the spaces between plants. These plants are chosen for their architectural shape, fine texture and the disciplined repetition that defines a contemporary planting.
style-foundation: Foundation planting frames the front of a house, softening the join between building and garden and giving a tidy, settled look year round. Because it is on view in every season and at close range, it leans heavily on evergreens and reliable, low-maintenance shrubs that hold their shape without constant attention. Keep taller plants clear of windows and allow for mature spread so you are not forever cutting back from the walls. Repeat a few well-chosen plants for a calm, cohesive frontage rather than a one-of-everything collection. Vary leaf texture and add seasonal flower for relief. These plants are chosen for dependable structure and good manners close to the house, the kind that look composed every month of the year.
style-shade_cottage: A shaded cottage border keeps the romantic, abundant spirit of the traditional cottage garden but swaps the sun-loving roses and delphiniums for plants that flower happily out of direct light. The principle is the same, generous, informal, densely planted with self-seeders allowed to wander, but the palette draws on woodland-edge favourites: foxgloves, hardy geraniums, columbines, hellebores and primroses, lifted with plenty of pale flower to glow in the gloom. Enrich the soil with leaf mould and keep it moist. The mistake is forcing full-sun cottage staples into shade, where they grow leggy and shy. These plants give that soft, overflowing cottage look in a north or east-facing border, or under the dappling of trees.
style-xeriscape: A low-water border is designed to thrive on rainfall alone once established, which makes it both drought-proof and low-maintenance, but it relies on getting the soil right. Counter-intuitively, sharp drainage matters more than fertility: most drought-tolerant plants come from lean, stony ground and rot in rich, damp soil, so add grit and gravel rather than compost, and mulch with stone chippings to keep roots cool and weeds down. Water new plants through their first summer only, then leave them to root deep. Grey, hairy, waxy and succulent leaves are the signs of plants built to cope. These plants are chosen to flourish with little or no watering, for gravel gardens and hot, dry banks.
style-meadow: A meadow border captures the loose, naturalistic drift of a wildflower field: grasses woven through perennials in informal sweeps, plants allowed to mingle and self-seed, with the eye carried across the planting rather than stopped at neat blocks. The crucial and most-missed point is fertility, as meadow plants need lean soil; on rich ground the grasses and thugs swamp the flowers, so do not feed or improve it. Plant in interlocking groups rather than clumps, mixing flower and grass, and cut back once in late winter to leave seed heads and structure standing. These plants are chosen for that prairie-meadow effect, combining airy grasses with long-flowering perennials that knit into a self-sustaining tapestry.
style-coastal: A coastal border faces a particular set of trials: salt-laden wind, fierce sun, free-draining sandy soil and sheer exposure. Plants that cope share telltale features, grey, waxy, leathery or hairy leaves that resist salt burn and reduce water loss, and many are wind-pruned into tough, low mounds. The first priority is a windbreak or shelter belt of resilient shrubs to take the brunt, behind which more tender planting can shelter. Improve sandy soil with organic matter to hold moisture, and avoid tall, brittle plants that snap. These plants are chosen to withstand wind and salt spray, from front-line toughs that shrug off the gales to flowering choices for the calmer ground behind them.
style-formal: A formal border depends on symmetry, clean lines and clipped structure, where the satisfaction comes from order and repetition rather than floral abundance. Evergreen shrubs that take regular clipping provide the architecture, defining edges, framing focal points and holding the design through winter when looser planting has gone. Geometry and balance are everything, so plant in matched pairs and repeated rhythms, and keep the palette disciplined. Within the clipped framework, restrained planting in blocks or standards adds detail without breaking the calm. The mistake is letting informality creep in and blur the lines. These plants are chosen for crisp structure, clippability and the poised, architectural quality that a formal scheme requires.
style-mediterranean: A Mediterranean border evokes the dry, sun-baked hillsides of southern Europe: aromatic, silver-leaved, drought-tolerant planting set among gravel and warm stone. The single most important thing is drainage, as these plants rot in cold, wet winter soil, so plant on a free-draining or raised bed, add plenty of grit, and mulch with gravel rather than bark. Choose a hot, sheltered spot, plant in spring, and water sparingly only while establishing. Many of these plants are culinary and aromatic herbs whose scent is released in the heat. The mistake is rich soil and overwatering. These plants are chosen for the sun-loving, silvery, fragrant character of a Mediterranean scheme, built to relish heat and shrug off drought.
low-edging: Front-of-border and edging plants, broadly those under 40cm, soften the line where a bed meets path or lawn and stop the planting looking like it stops abruptly at a wall. The job is to flow over the edge a little, blurring the boundary, so favour low mounds, spreading mats and front-runners rather than stiff, upright plants. Plant in continuous drifts or repeated groups along the front so the edge reads as deliberate, not patchy. Keep these the shortest layer, with the bed rising in tiers behind, or you lose the sense of depth. These plants are chosen to furnish the very front of a border, from neat clipped mounds to loose, tumbling spreaders that knit along the edge.
mid-border: The middle tier, roughly 40 to 100cm, is the body of the border and where most of the flowering happens; get this layer right and the whole bed works. These plants sit between the low front edging and the tall back-of-border specimens, so they need enough height to be seen over the front planting without blocking what stands behind. Plant in interlocking drifts that overlap their neighbours by flowering time, so as one group fades another rises through it. Repeat a few key plants along the bed to give rhythm and stop it looking like a collection of one-offs. These plants occupy that workhorse mid-height band, the long-flowering perennials and compact shrubs that carry a border through the season.
tall-back: Back-of-border plants, over 100cm, give a bed its height, backdrop and sense of enclosure, drawing the eye up and setting off everything in front. Place them at the rear of a one-sided border or down the spine of an island bed, and check the eventual height against what they will stand against, as a tall plant lost against a dark fence is wasted. Many need staking before they need it, so support them early rather than trying to rescue a flopped clump after a summer storm. Allow room to get behind them for maintenance. These plants are chosen to form the tallest layer, from airy see-through screens to solid structural giants that anchor the back of the bed.
shrubs-for-shade: Shrubs that tolerate shade solve one of the trickiest problems in a garden: giving a shaded border permanent structure and bulk when most flowering shrubs demand full sun. The hardest case is dry shade under trees, where shrubs must compete with thirsty roots, so dig in plenty of leaf mould and organic matter and water faithfully through the first two or three summers until they establish. Many shade shrubs earn their place on foliage and form rather than a brief flush of flower, with glossy evergreens particularly valuable for lifting a dark corner year round. The mistake is expecting heavy bloom in deep shade. These shrubs are selected to give reliable structure and presence out of direct sun.
perennials-for-full-sun: Sun-loving perennials are the most generous flowerers in the garden, repaying an open, south or west-facing position with months of bloom, but the brightest spots also dry fastest and many of these plants prefer lean soil to rich. Overfeeding gives lush, floppy growth that flops and needs staking, so go easy on the compost and let them earn their keep. Plant in bold drifts, deadhead to extend flowering, and water deeply but infrequently to push roots down to find their own moisture. Pair them with grasses for movement and a long season. The mistake is crowding, which traps damp air and invites mildew. These perennials are chosen to flower hard and long in a hot, sunny border.
pollinator-plants-for-shade: Most advice on feeding bees and butterflies assumes a sunny border, which leaves shaded gardens short of guidance, yet plenty of nectar-rich plants flower happily out of direct sun. The trick is timing: shade under deciduous trees is brightest in early spring before the canopy closes, so this is the moment for early-flowering shade plants that feed the first bumblebees and emerging pollinators when little else is open. Through the shaded summer, lean on the woodland-edge flowers that keep producing nectar in dappled light. Plant in drifts so foragers do not waste energy, and avoid sterile double flowers. These plants combine genuine shade tolerance with real value to pollinators, for a border that feeds insects out of the sun.
evergreen-shrubs: Evergreen shrubs are the most valuable plants in the garden for year-round structure, holding their leaves and their shape through the bleak months when everything else has died back to the ground. Use them to anchor a border, screen a boundary, frame a view or repeat down a bed as a unifying thread, and remember they read at full strength in winter when you most want substance outside. Plant in autumn or spring and water through the first year, as they transpire even in cold weather and can scorch in a dry, windy winter. Vary leaf size, colour and the gold or silver forms to avoid a flat green wall. These shrubs hold their leaves all year, from clippable backbone plants to lower furnishing evergreens.
plants-for-clay-shade: Clay shade combines two of the most awkward conditions in one border: heavy, cold, slow-draining soil and a lack of direct light, often in the damp shadow on the north side of a house or under trees. The plants that cope are a tough and specific group, tolerant of soil that stays wet in winter and dry in a tree's summer rain shadow alike, and they tend to rely on bold foliage rather than sun-hungry flower. Never work clay when it is wet, open it up with grit and organic matter, and plant slightly proud so crowns do not sit in cold water. These plants are chosen to thrive in exactly that combination of heavy soil and shade where so many others sulk or rot.
